title: Mắm Tôm
subtitle: vietnamese fermented shrimp sauce
excerpt: Mắm tôm is a pungent Vietnamese condiment made from fermented shrimp paste diluted with lime juice, sugar, and chilli into a dipping sauce. It is a bold, deeply savoury sauce used with bún đậu mắm tôm and other northern dishes. This recipe makes about 150ml.
sourceNotes: Mắm tôm is one of the most pungent condiments in Vietnamese cooking and is essential to northern Vietnamese food culture. The fermented shrimp paste is made commercially and diluted at home to make the dipping sauce.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a larger batch and keep in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made up to a week ahead and kept refrigerated. The flavour mellows slightly over time.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fermented shrimp paste from Vietnam, with a very strong smell and intensely savoury, slightly funky flavour. It comes in jars and is sold at Asian supermarkets. A little goes a long way.
A popular northern Vietnamese dish of rice vermicelli, fried tofu, and pork served with mắm tôm dipping sauce. It is one of the most iconic uses of the shrimp paste condiment.

content.text: Mắm tôm sauce starts with
mắm tôm
fermented shrimp paste, which is diluted and brightened with lime juice and sugar to make a dipping sauce.
It is the essential sauce for
bún đậu mắm tôm
and many other northern dishes.
This recipe makes about 150ml.
The smell of mắm tôm is very strong. Open a window when heating it. The flavour is much more nuanced than the aroma suggests.
What you need

items.prepNote: use fermented shrimp paste (mắm tôm) - available in jars at Asian supermarkets

content.text: Method
Heat the vegetable oil in a small saucepan over low heat. Add the minced lemongrass and garlic. Fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add 2 tablespoons of fermented shrimp paste to the pan. Stir over low heat for 1 minute until warmed through. The heat reduces the raw edge of the paste.
Remove from heat. Add the lime juice and sugar. Stir well until the sugar dissolves.
Add the sliced chilli. Taste the sauce. It should be pungent, salty, slightly sweet, and sour. Adjust the lime and sugar to your preference.
Transfer to a small dipping bowl. Serve at room temperature alongside tofu, vermicelli, boiled pork, or any dish that calls for it.

attrs.symptom: The sauce is far too pungent and overpowering.
attrs.cause: Too much shrimp paste was used or the paste was not warmed first.
attrs.fix: Warm the paste in oil before adding lime - this mellows its raw edge significantly. Start with 1 tablespoon and build up from there.

attrs.symptom: The sauce is too thick and pasty.
attrs.cause: Not enough lime juice or the shrimp paste is very dense.
attrs.fix: Add more lime juice a teaspoon at a time. You can also add a tablespoon of warm water to loosen the sauce to a dipping consistency.

attrs.symptom: The shrimp paste is difficult to find locally.
attrs.cause: Mắm tôm is a specialist ingredient not stocked in all supermarkets.
attrs.fix: Look for it at Vietnamese or Chinese supermarkets. It comes in a purple-grey jar. Belachan (Malaysian shrimp paste) can substitute in a pinch but has a different texture.

content.text: Where this dish lives
Mắm tôm is a cornerstone condiment of northern Vietnamese cooking.
It divides opinion sharply . northerners consider it an essential flavour, while southerners often find it too strong.
The paste is produced in coastal areas of the north where shrimp are fermented in large vats.
As a dipping sauce it is especially associated with bún đậu mắm tôm, one of Hanoi's most beloved street foods.
For those who love it, no substitution is acceptable.
